decks.title: SFM: Financial Derivatives, Instruments for Risk Management
decks.description: Recall cards for CMA Final Paper 14, Chapter 13: forwards, futures and hedging, options and strategies, option pricing and the Greeks, swaps and interest rate derivatives.

fields.definition_md: A contract that has no standalone value. Its worth is entirely driven by the price of something else, the underlying, which may be a security, commodity, bullion, currency, livestock or almost any other asset.
A derivative whose underlying is a financial asset or measure: securities, security indexes, reference rates, or a combination of these. The other broad family is commodity derivatives.

fields.prompt_md: Name the four economic functions performed by a derivatives market.
fields.answer_md: Price discovery, transfer of risk, higher liquidity and trading volume in the underlying market, and wider participation (including new entrepreneurial activity).

fields.prompt_md: How does a derivatives market help in price discovery, and what happens to derivative and underlying prices at expiry?
fields.answer_md: Derivative prices reflect what participants expect the future to look like, so they pull the underlying toward that expected level and reveal both current and future prices. At expiry the derivative price converges with the price of the underlying.

fields.prompt_md: In what sense is a derivatives market a risk-transfer mechanism?
fields.answer_md: It moves risk away from those who hold it but dislike it (hedgers) towards those who are willing to carry it for a possible reward (speculators and other risk-takers).

fields.prompt_md: Why does introducing derivatives tend to raise trading volume in the underlying cash market?
fields.answer_md: More players enter because they can now offload the risk through derivatives; without such an arrangement many of them would stay out. The linkage between the two markets then lifts activity in the cash market as well.

fields.prompt_md: List the basic features shared by derivative contracts.
fields.answer_md: A binding contract between two parties to be performed in future; value derived from an underlying asset; specified obligations for each party; can be struck directly (OTC) or through an exchange; usually carried off the balance sheet; and mostly secondary-market instruments.

fields.prompt_md: How are most derivative positions closed out, and why are they called deferred delivery or deferred payment instruments?
fields.answer_md: Usually the underlying is not delivered; the position is settled by taking an offsetting position in the derivative itself. Delivery or payment is pushed to a later date, which is why taking a long or short position is easier than in the underlying asset.

fields.prompt_md: What is the notional amount of a derivative contract, and how does it relate to the contract's payoff?
fields.answer_md: The notional amount sets the size of the contract. Because the actual payoff is only a small part of that figure, derivatives sit off the balance sheet and the payoff differs from what the notional amount alone would suggest.

fields.prompt_md: State the main benefits of using financial derivatives.
fields.answer_md: Cheaper management of business risk, lower financing costs for end-users, access to markets that would otherwise be costly or unfamiliar, lower transaction costs than the spot market for asset management, scope to exploit tax and regulatory differences across markets, and the ability to speculate.

fields.prompt_md: Name the four basic (plain) derivative contracts and give a one-line description of each.
fields.answer_md: Forward: customised OTC deal to buy or sell at a pre-agreed price on a future date. Future: standardised, exchange-traded version of a forward. Option: right but not the obligation to buy or sell at a strike price. Swap: private agreement to exchange cash flows by a set formula.

fields.expands_md: Forwards, Futures, Options, Swaps: the four basic derivatives.

fields.prompt_md: What are complex derivatives? Give four examples.
fields.answer_md: Derivatives built from two or more other derivatives. Examples: warrants, LEAPS, basket options and swaptions.

fields.definition_md: A longer-dated option, traded over the counter. Listed options usually live for up to a year (most exchange-traded ones have a maximum life of about nine months), so anything longer is called a warrant.
Long-term Equity Anticipation Securities: options on equity with a maturity of up to three years.
An option written on a portfolio of underlying assets rather than on one asset. The underlying is usually a moving average of the basket, and equity index options are a form of basket option.
An option to buy or sell a swap that becomes operative when the option expires.

fields.prompt_md: Classify financial derivatives by the underlying asset.
fields.answer_md: Equity derivatives (stock and index futures and options), interest rate derivatives, foreign exchange derivatives and credit derivatives.

fields.prompt_md: Which instruments fall under foreign exchange derivatives?
fields.answer_md: Currency forwards, currency futures, currency swaps, currency options and foreign exchange binary options. They are used to hedge exchange risk, speculate on currencies or arbitrage.

fields.prompt_md: Which instruments are credit derivatives?
fields.answer_md: Contracts whose value depends on the creditworthiness of, or a credit event at, a referenced entity: credit default swaps, collateralised debt obligations, total return swaps, options on credit default swaps and credit spread forwards.

fields.prompt_md: Which authority regulates which derivatives in India, according to the study text?
fields.answer_md: The RBI regulates interest rate, foreign currency and credit derivatives; the other types come under SEBI.

fields.definition_md: A tailor-made agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset on a set future date at a price fixed today. It is traded over the counter, typically between two financial institutions or an institution and its client, not on an exchange.

fields.prompt_md: Describe the main features of a forward contract.
fields.answer_md: Bilateral and so exposed to counterparty default; custom designed in asset, quality, size and expiry; one party is long (buyer) and the other short (seller); settled by delivery on the expiry date; very popular in currencies and interest-rate instruments.

fields.prompt_md: Distinguish delivery price from forward price in a forward contract.
fields.answer_md: The delivery price is the price written into the contract and never changes. The forward price is the delivery price that would apply to a contract started today. The two are equal when the contract is signed; afterwards the forward price keeps moving while the delivery price stays put.

fields.prompt_md: Name the four kinds of forward contract by underlying.
fields.answer_md: Commodity forwards (such as gold), currency forwards, equity forwards (a stock, portfolio or index) and interest rate forwards.

fields.definition_md: The long side agrees to buy the underlying at the future date; the short side agrees to sell it. Spot price is the price for immediate delivery; the future spot price is the spot price on the contract's expiry date.

fields.name: Payoff of a forward contract at expiry
fields.variables_md: $P_T$ = spot price at delivery date; $K$ = agreed forward (delivery) price.
fields.when_md: Both sides break even when $P_T = K$. The long side has unlimited gain and loses at most $K$; the short side gains at most $K$ and has unlimited loss.

fields.prompt_md: A forward buyer's profit and loss pattern versus the seller's: who gains when the spot price rises?
fields.answer_md: The buyer (long) gains when the spot price at expiry exceeds the agreed price; the seller (short) gains when it falls below. The two payoffs are mirror images and sum to zero.

fields.prompt_md: What advantages do forward contracts offer?
fields.answer_md: They lock in the price of a future purchase or sale, need no upfront premium, and being tailor-made can hedge exposure up to 100%, which standardised futures or options often cannot.

fields.prompt_md: What limitations make forwards less attractive?
fields.answer_md: No centralised trading system (OTC), no organised secondary market so they are illiquid, and with no exchange as intermediary there is substantial counterparty risk.

fields.prompt_md: Under the study text, into which three categories did the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952 place forward contracts?
fields.answer_md: Hedge contracts, transferable specific delivery contracts and non-transferable specific delivery contracts.

fields.definition_md: A standardised, exchange-listed contract that obliges one side to buy and the other to sell a given underlying on a fixed future date, at the price agreed today. That agreed price is the futures price, the closing date is the delivery or final settlement date, and the underlying's quoted price on that date is the settlement price.

fields.prompt_md: List the characteristics that make a futures contract different from a forward.
fields.answer_md: Exchange traded, available only on selected assets, standardised terms, a clearing house as counterparty to every trade, daily marking to market, margin deposits, mostly cash settlement, exchange-fixed delivery and expiry, and regulation of the market.

fields.prompt_md: What does standardisation of a futures contract cover?
fields.answer_md: Quantity (the lot size), quality of the underlying, the delivery date and month, and the minimum price movement (tick). A trader cannot choose a different date or lot.

fields.prompt_md: What role does the clearing house play in futures trading?
fields.answer_md: It stands between buyer and seller, acting as the counterparty to every trade: the buyer effectively buys from it and the seller sells to it. It keeps accounts, collects margins and settles deliveries, which greatly reduces counterparty risk.

fields.prompt_md: Why are many futures contracts, such as index futures, cash settled?
fields.answer_md: Delivery of the underlying is often inconvenient or impossible (an index cannot be delivered). The long or short instead pays cash equal to the difference between the contract price and the price at expiry.

fields.prompt_md: List the types of futures by underlying.
fields.answer_md: Stock futures, index futures, currency futures and interest rate futures.

fields.definition_md: A stock future commits the parties to buy or sell a fixed number of shares of one stock at a set price on a set date. An index future is a contract on the face value of an index, which is the index level multiplied by a fixed rupee amount per point.

fields.prompt_md: On what underlying do interest rate futures trade at NSE, and how are they settled (per the study text)?
fields.answer_md: Government securities (bonds of 6, 10 and 13 years) and the 91-day Treasury Bill. All futures at NSE are cash settled.

fields.definition_md: Futures price minus spot price. In a normal market it is positive because carrying costs lift the futures price. It shrinks as expiry nears, and the two prices converge.

fields.prompt_md: Normal market versus inverted market: what is the sign of the basis?
fields.answer_md: Normal market: futures price above spot, basis positive (this is also called contango). Inverted market: spot above futures, basis negative (backwardation).

fields.prompt_md: Explain the three hypotheses on the futures-spot relationship: normal backwardation, contango and the expectation principle.
fields.answer_md: Normal backwardation: futures price is a downward-biased estimate of the later spot price (expected basis negative). Contango: speculators bid prices up, leaving a positive basis. Expectation principle: futures price is an unbiased estimate of expected spot, so the expected basis is zero and no excess return exists for hedgers or speculators.

fields.prompt_md: Compare forwards and futures on standardisation, trading venue, liquidity, margin and settlement.
fields.answer_md: Forwards: negotiated terms, OTC, illiquid, no margin, settled once at expiry (often by delivery). Futures: standard terms, exchange traded, liquid, margin required, settled daily and normally in cash.

fields.prompt_md: How do forwards and futures differ in transaction cost and in how much of the contract ends in physical delivery?
fields.answer_md: Forward dealers earn through the bid-ask spread, while futures carry brokerage; around 90 per cent of forwards end in actual delivery against very few futures.

fields.definition_md: At the end of each trading day every open futures contract is repriced at that day's settlement price. Losers' margin accounts are debited and gainers' accounts credited, which cuts the risk of default compared with forwards.

fields.prompt_md: Illustrate daily settlement: a long position in a futures lot of 250 shares bought at 2,100 and the price closes at 2,150.
fields.answer_md: Profit that day is (2,150 - 2,100) x 250 = Rs 12,500, credited immediately. The old contract is cancelled and replaced by a fresh one at the new price of 2,150.

fields.definition_md: The deposit a trader must place with the broker to open a futures position, acting as a good-faith deposit. The exchange sets it from the past volatility of the underlying so that the clearing house is covered even in the worst expected day; it is roughly the maximum permitted daily price move.
The minimum balance that must stay in the margin account. If the balance drops below it, the broker issues a margin call.
The extra money the trader pays after a margin call to bring the account back up to the initial margin level (not just back to the maintenance level).

fields.prompt_md: Initial margin Rs 5,000, maintenance margin Rs 3,750 (75% of initial). After losses of 1,000 and then 500 the balance is 3,500. What happens?
fields.answer_md: The balance has gone below maintenance margin, so the broker makes a margin call and the trader must deposit enough to restore Rs 5,000, the initial margin level. That deposit (Rs 1,500) is the variation margin.

fields.prompt_md: Why does the exchange require margin from both buyer and seller of a futures contract?
fields.answer_md: Margin acts as collateral against failure by either party, so a defaulting trader's own deposit absorbs the loss before the clearing house is exposed.

fields.prompt_md: Differences between futures contracts and options on the point of who must perform.
fields.answer_md: In a futures contract both buyer and seller are obliged to perform; in an option only the writer (seller) is obliged, the holder having a right but no obligation.

fields.prompt_md: How does continuous compounding differ from periodic compounding for a sum P at rate r for n years?
fields.answer_md: With $m$ compounding periods a year the sum becomes $P(1+r/m)^{mn}$. As compounding becomes continuous it becomes $Pe^{rn}$, and the present-value factor $(1+r)^{-n}$ is replaced by $e^{-rn}$. Rs 10,000 at 10% for 2 years is Rs 12,100 annually compounded but about Rs 12,214 continuously compounded.

fields.name: Continuous compounding and discounting
fields.variables_md: $r$ = annual rate (continuous), $t$ = years, $e \approx 2.71828$.
fields.when_md: Used for every derivative-pricing formula in this chapter: forward and futures prices, option minimum values, put-call parity and swap valuation.

fields.definition_md: Prices a forward or futures contract so that no arbitrage is possible: futures price = spot price + cost of carrying the asset - income earned on holding it. Carrying costs include interest on funds used (or forgone), and for commodities storage and insurance; carry return is income such as dividends.

fields.prompt_md: What is arbitrage?
fields.answer_md: A trade that earns a risk-free profit without any cash outlay. In a well-working market it should not last, but transaction costs and other imperfections can let actual prices drift from theoretical values.

fields.prompt_md: State the assumptions behind the cost of carry model.
fields.answer_md: Perfect markets; no transaction costs; assets infinitely divisible; no bid-ask spread (a single price); no limits on short selling and short sellers can use the full proceeds; traders act on arbitrage opportunities as soon as they arise.

fields.prompt_md: Notation used in cost of carry pricing: what do S, F*, F, K, r and T stand for?
fields.answer_md: S = spot price today; F* = theoretical (fair) forward or futures price; F = actual quoted price; K = delivery price in the contract; r = risk-free rate per year; T (or t) = time left to delivery.

fields.name: Forward or futures price: asset with no income
fields.variables_md: $S_0$ = spot price, $r$ = continuously compounded risk-free rate, $t$ = years to maturity.
fields.when_md: Non-dividend paying shares and discount bonds.

fields.name: Forward or futures price: asset paying known cash income
fields.variables_md: $I$ = present value of the cash income (for example dividends) received during the contract life; $D_k$ is each payment, $t_k$ its timing.
fields.when_md: Stocks with a known dividend, coupon bonds, and an index where the dividends are known in amount. First reduce spot by the PV of the income, then compound.

fields.name: Forward or futures price: asset paying a known yield
fields.variables_md: $y$ = income yield per year, assumed paid continuously.
fields.when_md: Stock indices, where dividends are expressed as a percentage of the index level.

fields.name: Futures price with storage cost
fields.expression_md: $F^{*} = S_0\,e^{(r+c)t}$ if storage is a % of price; $F^{*}=(S_0+U)e^{rt}$ if storage is a cash amount
fields.variables_md: $c$ = storage cost as a % of price per year; $U$ = present value of storage costs paid during the life.
fields.when_md: Commodities such as metals or raw materials. For storage paid later, add its present value to the spot price before compounding.

fields.prompt_md: Compute the theoretical 6-month forward price of a non-dividend share at Rs 100 when the risk-free rate is 10% continuously compounded.
A share at Rs 200 will pay a Rs 5 dividend in 3 months. Risk-free rate is 8%. Find the 6-month forward price.
An index stands at 1,000, risk-free rate is 9% and the index yield is 4%. Find the 3-month futures price.
A commodity is Rs 75 per kg, storage costs 4% p.a., risk-free rate 12%. Price a 3-month futures contract.
The quoted futures price exceeds the cost-of-carry price: which arbitrage position is taken?
fields.answer_md: Futures are overvalued: buy the asset in the spot market (funded by borrowing) and sell the futures. This is cash-and-carry arbitrage. At expiry deliver or sell at the futures price, repay the loan with interest and keep the difference.

fields.prompt_md: Futures trade at a discount to the theoretical price: how is the mispricing exploited?
fields.answer_md: Futures are undervalued: short-sell the asset, invest the proceeds at the risk-free rate and buy futures. At expiry take delivery to close the short sale. This is reverse cash-and-carry.

fields.prompt_md: Spot Rs 100, theoretical 6-month futures Rs 105.13 (r = 10%). The futures actually trade at Rs 108. Show the arbitrage gain.
fields.answer_md: Borrow Rs 100, buy the share, sell the futures at 108. At expiry the loan has grown to 100 x $e^0.05$ = 105.13. Delivering the share earns 108, so the locked-in profit is about Rs 2.87 per share.

fields.prompt_md: Same data, but the futures trade at Rs 103. What is the arbitrage gain?
fields.answer_md: Short sell at 100 and invest it, which grows to 105.13. Buy futures at 103 and use the share received to close the short position, giving a risk-free gain of about Rs 2.13.

fields.prompt_md: Outline the steps to find the theoretical price of an index or stock future that has an expected dividend.
fields.answer_md: 1) Discount each dividend to today at the risk-free rate. 2) Subtract that PV from spot to get the adjusted spot. 3) Compound the adjusted spot to expiry at the risk-free rate. 4) Compare with the quoted futures price and act: sell futures and buy spot if quoted is higher, otherwise the reverse.

fields.name: Value of a forward contract after inception
fields.variables_md: $F^*$ = current forward price for the same maturity, $K$ = delivery price fixed in the contract.
fields.when_md: Its value at inception is zero. Afterwards it can become positive or negative as the forward price moves.

fields.prompt_md: Forward price of a futures contract versus its forward counterpart: when do they differ?
fields.answer_md: In a perfect market with unchanged interest rates they are equal. With variable rates, if futures prices move with interest rates (positive correlation) futures tend to price above forwards; with a negative correlation they price below. Frictions such as transaction costs and taxes weaken this, so futures are usually taken to equal the cost-of-carry forward price.

fields.prompt_md: Why is a stock future priced like a stock forward?
fields.answer_md: The same cost of carry formula applies to both, so the formula is not repeated for stock futures. Index futures use the same three cases (no dividend, known dividend, known dividend yield).

fields.definition_md: A position taken in a second asset to protect the value of one already held. A hedge aims to lock in the value that existed when it was set up, not to make a profit or reduce a loss; if the feared event does not happen it brings no gain.

fields.prompt_md: When hedging with a correlated asset, should you buy or sell it?
fields.answer_md: If the hedging asset moves in the same direction as the asset you hold (positive correlation) you sell it, so that its gain on a price fall offsets the loss on your holding. If it moves oppositely (negative correlation) you buy it.

fields.prompt_md: Can a hedge be partial? What is the effect?
fields.answer_md: Yes. A manager can protect, say, 50% or 75% of the exposure. Only that share of a fall is covered; the rest of the loss stays with the holder (and the rest of any gain too).

fields.prompt_md: Why should the hedger hedge only when an adverse move is expected?
fields.answer_md: If the unfavourable event never occurs the hedge gives nothing and merely freezes the value that existed on the day it was set up, giving up the chance of gain. A hedge is therefore only worth taking when the adverse event is genuinely feared.

fields.prompt_md: How do you hedge a stock or portfolio you already own using futures, and which direction is the futures position?
fields.answer_md: Take an equal and opposite position in futures: sell futures against a long holding. For a 100% hedge the futures value equals the holding; for a part hedge, a proportionate amount. If the market rallies the gain is given up, but a market fall is covered.

fields.prompt_md: When is beta relevant in hedging with futures?
fields.answer_md: If you hedge a stock with futures on the same stock, beta does not matter because both move together. If you hedge a stock or portfolio with index futures, the beta of the holding relative to the index must be used, because the holding may be more or less volatile than the market.

fields.name: Index futures needed for a hedge
fields.variables_md: $V$ = portfolio value, $\beta$ = portfolio beta against the index, $h$ = proportion hedged (1 for full hedge), denominator = value of one futures contract.
fields.when_md: Sell this many contracts to protect a long portfolio. The total futures value should equal beta times the portfolio value.

fields.prompt_md: Portfolio of Rs 67.50 crore, beta 1.5, hedged 100% with Nifty futures quoted at 4,500, lot 100 units. How many contracts, and what happens if the market moves 10%?
fields.answer_md: Each contract is worth 4,500 x 100 = Rs 4.5 lakh. Futures value required = 1.5 x 67.50 = Rs 101.25 crore, so sell 2,250 contracts. If the market falls 10%, the portfolio falls 15% (Rs 10.125 crore) while the short futures gain 10% of Rs 101.25 crore (Rs 10.125 crore), so the net result is nil; a 10% rise is offset in the same way.

fields.prompt_md: Same portfolio but only 50% is hedged. What changes?
fields.answer_md: Protection is halved: when the market falls the futures gain covers only half of the portfolio's loss, so the net result is not zero.

fields.prompt_md: How can a fund holding cash use index futures when it expects a rally?
fields.answer_md: Buy index futures now to take part in the rally; only a small margin (about 10% of value in the study text's example) is blocked and the balance can earn money-market returns. When the stock list is ready, close the futures and buy the shares. If no rally occurs, shares are bought cheaper.

fields.prompt_md: Which risk can stock index futures hedge, and which not?
fields.answer_md: They hedge systematic (market) risk, letting an investor keep the stock-specific return while shedding market risk. They do nothing for the unsystematic risk of an individual stock.

fields.name: Futures needed to change portfolio beta
fields.variables_md: $V$ = portfolio value, $\beta$ = existing beta, $\beta^{*}$ = desired beta. Derived from $V\beta \pm \text{Futures} = V\beta^{*}$.
fields.when_md: Positive N: buy futures to raise beta (bullish view). Negative N: sell futures to cut beta (bearish view). Use the portfolio value that carries the beta, including any cash at zero beta.

fields.prompt_md: Reduce beta of Rs 67.50 crore portfolio from 1.5 to 1.0 using Nifty futures of Rs 4.5 lakh each. What to do?
fields.answer_md: Futures value to sell = 67.50 x (1.5 - 1.0) = Rs 33.75 crore, which is 33.75 crore / 4.5 lakh = 750 contracts sold. With a 10% fall the portfolio loses 10.125 crore, futures gain 3.375 crore, net loss 6.75 crore (the loss of a beta-1 portfolio).

fields.prompt_md: Rs 100 crore portfolio (Rs 80 crore equity plus Rs 20 crore cash), beta 1.2, wants beta of 0.8. Index future 5,500, lot 100. How many contracts?
fields.answer_md: One contract = 5,500 x 100 = Rs 5.5 lakh. $N=(0.8-1.2)\times100\text{ crore}/5.5\text{ lakh}\approx -727$. A negative number means sell about 727 contracts.

fields.prompt_md: How is the beta of a multi-stock portfolio found, and how is it then moved to a target?
fields.answer_md: Beta of the portfolio is the value-weighted average of the stock betas. For shares worth 16, 24 and 12 crore with betas 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 it is about 1.19 on Rs 52 crore. To reach 0.8 with a Rs 2.7 lakh index contract sell about 751 contracts; to reach 1.5 buy about 597.

fields.definition_md: The number of futures contracts held for a given position in the underlying, expressed as futures position divided by underlying position. Using index futures for a perfect hedge, the hedge ratio equals the beta of the portfolio. Using same-stock futures it is 1; below 1 is a partial hedge, above 1 an over-hedge.

fields.name: Beta as correlation times volatility ratio
fields.variables_md: $\rho_{SF}$ = correlation between the asset's price change and the futures price change; $\sigma_S,\sigma_F$ = standard deviations of the changes in spot and futures price.
fields.when_md: Index futures are treated as a proxy for the market, so beta is also the minimum-variance hedge ratio.

fields.prompt_md: Portfolio of Rs 50 crore with beta 1.2: what hedge ratio results from selling futures of Rs 60, 30 and 120 crore?
fields.answer_md: Ratio = futures value / portfolio value: 1.2 (60 crore, a full 100% hedge, equal to beta), 0.6 (30 crore, a 50% hedge) and 2.4 (120 crore, a 200% hedge, over-hedged).

fields.definition_md: Hedging a cash position by taking the opposite position in futures on a different but related stock or index, used when the asset to be protected has no futures market. Basis risk is built in because the spot and futures prices belong to different assets and need not converge.

fields.name: Cross hedge ratio and number of contracts
fields.expression_md: $h = \rho_{SF}\dfrac{\sigma_S}{\sigma_F} \qquad N = h\times\dfrac{\text{units to hedge}}{\text{units per contract}}$
fields.variables_md: $h$ = hedge ratio (also the beta of the asset against the hedging instrument).
fields.when_md: Example: hedge ratio 1.2, 1,000 shares, 100 units per index contract: N = 1.2 x 1,000 / 100 = 12 contracts.

fields.prompt_md: Among several possible cross-hedge instruments how is the best one chosen?
fields.answer_md: Prefer the instrument whose price change is most highly correlated with the asset being hedged. If two instruments have the same beta, take the one with higher correlation; the study text also notes that a lower or nearer-to-1 beta may be preferred when correlations tie.

fields.prompt_md: Perfect hedge versus imperfect hedge.
fields.answer_md: A perfect hedge removes the price risk completely, covering 100% of the cash position with the opposite derivative position. An imperfect hedge covers it only partly or with an imperfect proxy.

fields.prompt_md: Rs 1.01 crore portfolio, beta 2.0, hedged with 4-month BSE index futures (index 50,000, 50 units per contract, futures about 50,500). How many contracts and what is the gain if the index falls to 45,000?
fields.answer_md: Contract value = 50 x 50,500 = Rs 25.25 lakh. N = 1.01 crore x 2.0 / 25.25 lakh = 8 contracts, sold. Gain per unit = 50,500 - 45,000 = 5,500; per contract 2.75 lakh; total Rs 22 lakh.

fields.prompt_md: A buyer needs a commodity in six months and buys futures to lock the price. If spot ends below the futures price, did the hedge fail?
fields.answer_md: No. A futures hedge removes the uncertainty about price, fixing the cost at the futures price; it does not guarantee a gain. A loss against the later spot price is the price of certainty, so it is wrong to conclude the hedge failed.

fields.prompt_md: Which index-futures position hedges each view: long cash holding expected to rise or fall, and short cash position?
fields.answer_md: A long holding is hedged by selling index futures (size = beta x value). A short cash position is hedged by buying index futures (size = beta x value). The hedge position is always opposite to the cash position, whatever the view on direction.

fields.definition_md: A contract giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a given quantity of the underlying at a fixed price on or before a future date. If the buyer exercises, the seller must perform.

fields.prompt_md: List the main features of an option contract.
fields.answer_md: The buyer has a right and the seller a possible commitment; the buyer pays a premium, even if the option is never exercised; the price at which the asset is bought or sold is the exercise (strike) price, fixed at the start; the option is exercised on or before a set expiry; and exchange-traded contracts have fixed size and tenure.

fields.definition_md: The price the buyer pays the seller (writer) for the right the option gives. The writer keeps it whether or not the option is exercised. On an exchange it is set by supply and demand.
The price at which the underlying is bought or sold if the option is exercised. For exchange-traded options the exchange fixes a series of strikes at regular intervals and the investor picks one.

fields.prompt_md: What is standardised in an exchange-traded option?
fields.answer_md: The strike prices on offer, the expiry dates and the contract (lot) size are all fixed by the exchange. Only the premium is free to move with demand and supply, and depends on strike, expiry and the spot price among other things.

fields.term: Buyer (holder) and writer (seller) of an option
fields.definition_md: The holder has agreed the right to buy or sell the underlying at the strike price. The writer has promised to sell (call) or buy (put) at that price if the holder exercises.

fields.prompt_md: Call option versus put option.
fields.answer_md: A call gives the holder the right to buy the underlying, and the writer must sell if it is exercised. A put gives the holder the right to sell, and the writer must buy.

fields.prompt_md: American option versus European option.
fields.answer_md: An American option can be exercised at any time up to and including expiry; a European option only on the expiry date.

fields.prompt_md: Classify options by underlying asset.
fields.answer_md: Stock options, index options (for example on the Nifty 50), currency options and interest rate options.

fields.prompt_md: What distinguishes an option from a forward or future?
fields.answer_md: The right-but-not-obligation feature. Forward and futures bind both buyer and seller, whereas the option holder can walk away from an unfavourable deal. The option writer has no such right to refuse.

fields.prompt_md: Compare forwards, futures and options on the point of settlement and cash flows.
fields.answer_md: Forward: settled once, at the end, by delivery. Futures: profit or loss settled daily. Option: the writer collects the premium at the start; thereafter there is no daily settlement of price changes for the holder.

fields.prompt_md: Which of forward, future and option carry counterparty and liquidity risk?
fields.answer_md: Forwards (performance is not guaranteed). Futures and exchange-traded options are guaranteed by the exchange so counterparty and liquidity risk is little or none.

fields.prompt_md: State the main advantages and disadvantages of options.
fields.answer_md: Advantages: cheap access to the underlying, leverage, standardised and enforceable terms, hedging, return enhancement, and replicating a portfolio. Disadvantages: the option can expire worthless, leverage cuts both ways, writers of naked calls face unlimited risk, a wrong view on timing or direction spoils the hedge, and regulatory restrictions on exercise.

fields.definition_md: From the buyer's view: ITM means exercising would give a gain; ATM means exercising gives neither gain nor loss; OTM means exercising would cause a loss, so it is not exercised.

fields.prompt_md: State the moneyness conditions for a call and for a put using spot price S and exercise price X.
fields.answer_md: Call: S above X is ITM, S equal to X is ATM, S below X is OTM. Put: S below X is ITM, S equal to X is ATM, S above X is OTM.

fields.name: Net profit of an option buyer at expiry
fields.expression_md: $\text{Long call} = \max(S_T - X,\,0) - C \qquad \text{Long put} = \max(X - S_T,\,0) - P$
fields.variables_md: $S_T$ = spot price at expiry, $X$ = exercise price, $C$ and $P$ = call and put premium paid.
fields.when_md: The writer's net profit is the exact opposite: premium received less the buyer's gross gain.

fields.name: Break-even price of an option
fields.variables_md: $X$ = exercise price, $C$/$P$ = premium.
fields.when_md: At the break-even spot price the buyer's net profit is zero. Between the strike and the break-even point the option is ITM but the buyer still loses part of the premium.

fields.prompt_md: Summarise the maximum gain and loss for the buyer and the writer of a call and of a put.
fields.answer_md: Buyer of either option: maximum loss = premium; call gain unlimited, put gain up to (X minus premium) when the price falls to zero. Writer of either option: maximum gain = premium; call loss unlimited, put loss up to (X minus premium).

fields.prompt_md: A trader buys a call at strike Rs 2,620 for a premium of Rs 330. What is the break-even and what is the result at expiry prices of 2,390, 2,850, 2,950 and 3,050?
fields.answer_md: Break-even = 2,620 + 330 = Rs 2,950. At 2,390 the option lapses and he loses 330. At 2,850 he exercises and loses 100 net (230 gross less 330). At 2,950 net nil. At 3,050 profit is 100.

fields.prompt_md: A trader buys a put at strike Rs 1,380 for a premium of Rs 25. Find the break-even and the result at spot 1,410, 1,360, 1,355 and 1,345.
fields.answer_md: Break-even = 1,380 - 25 = Rs 1,355. At 1,410 the put lapses: loss of 25. At 1,360 gross gain is 20, net loss 5. At 1,355 net nil. At 1,345 net profit 10.

fields.prompt_md: Long call: view, risk and reward.
fields.answer_md: Bought when the trader expects the price to rise. Loss limited to the premium paid; profit potential unlimited; break-even at strike plus premium.

fields.prompt_md: Short call (call writing): view, risk and reward, and what is a naked call.
fields.answer_md: Written when the trader expects the price to fall or stay flat. Gain limited to the premium received; loss unlimited as the price rises. If the writer does not own the underlying it is a naked (uncovered) call, which has no protection against a rise.

fields.prompt_md: Long put: view, risk and reward.
fields.answer_md: Bought when the trader expects the price to fall. Loss limited to the premium paid; profit rises as the price falls, up to strike minus premium; break-even at strike minus premium.

fields.prompt_md: Short put (put writing): view, risk and reward, and what is a naked put.
fields.answer_md: Written when the trader expects the price to rise or hold. Gain limited to the premium received; loss grows as the price falls, up to strike minus premium. If the writer is not short or holding the stock it is a naked (uncovered) put.

fields.prompt_md: Why is the writer's payoff always the mirror image of the buyer's?
fields.answer_md: An option is a zero-sum contract: whatever the buyer gains at expiry the writer loses and vice versa, with the premium moving from buyer to writer at the start.

fields.definition_md: The gain from exercising immediately: for a call $\max(S-X,0)$, for a put $\max(X-S,0)$. An at-the-money or out-of-the-money option has zero intrinsic value. The concept is real for American options and only notional for European ones, which cannot be exercised early.

The part of the premium that exceeds intrinsic value (also called extrinsic value). It shrinks as expiry nears and is zero at expiry. For an ATM or OTM option the whole premium is time value; for an ITM option it is the premium less intrinsic value.

fields.prompt_md: A call with strike 1,380 trades at Rs 20. Spot is 1,390. Split the premium; then do the same at spot 1,350.
fields.answer_md: At 1,390: intrinsic value 10, time value 20 - 10 = 10 (option is ITM). At 1,350: intrinsic value 0 (OTM), so the whole Rs 20 is time value.

fields.prompt_md: Why are OTM and ATM options cheaper than ITM options, and what is the trade-off?
fields.answer_md: They have only time value and a bigger chance of expiring worthless, so premiums are lower. The flip side is a larger percentage gain if they do end up in the money.

fields.name: Minimum and maximum value of European options
fields.variables_md: $S$ = spot, $X$ = strike, $r$ = continuous risk-free rate, $t$ = years to expiry.
fields.when_md: Use to test whether a quoted premium is too low (arbitrage). For American options the maximum put value is $X$ and the minimum put value is $\max(0, X-S)$.

fields.prompt_md: Spot is Rs 185, strike Rs 200, six months to expiry, risk-free rate 5%. What is the minimum value of the European put, and what if the put is quoted at Rs 5?
fields.answer_md: Minimum = 200$e^{-0.025}$ - 185 = 195.06 - 185 = Rs 10.06. A quote of Rs 5 is below this, so the put is underpriced: borrow, buy the put and the stock, and exercise at expiry to lock in a profit (about Rs 5.19 in the study text's workings).

fields.prompt_md: How does the exercise price affect call and put premiums?
fields.answer_md: A higher strike lowers the call premium (less to gain from exercise) and raises the put premium. A lower strike raises the call premium and lowers the put premium.

fields.prompt_md: How does the spot price of the underlying affect premiums?
fields.answer_md: If the spot price rises the call premium rises and the put premium falls; if the spot price falls the put premium rises and the call premium falls.

fields.prompt_md: How do time to expiry and volatility affect option premiums?
fields.answer_md: Longer maturity means a longer period of uncertainty, so a higher premium (a 3-month option costs more than a 1-month one). Higher volatility lifts both call and put premiums because extreme prices are more likely and the writer's obligation can be larger.

fields.prompt_md: How do interest rates, dividends and market liquidity affect option premiums?
fields.answer_md: A rise in interest rates raises call values and lowers put values. A large expected dividend lowers call prices because the stock price falls when the dividend is paid. Liquidity in the market is the third market factor.

fields.text_md: Premium of an option rises with {{c1::time to expiry}} and {{c2::volatility}}; a higher strike makes a call {{c3::cheaper}} and a put {{c4::dearer}}.

fields.prompt_md: At expiry how does a holder decide whether to exercise or let an option lapse?
fields.answer_md: Compare the spot price with the strike. An ITM option (call: spot above strike; put: spot below strike) is exercised; an OTM option lapses; at the money, exercise makes no difference.

fields.prompt_md: Given strike, premium and market price you must identify unknowns in a table of options. How are break-even relationships used?
fields.answer_md: For calls, break-even = strike + premium, so any one of the three can be found from the other two. For puts, break-even = strike - premium. If the table says maximum gain and loss for the holder and writer are unlimited, the option is a call; if both are capped at strike minus premium, it is a put.

fields.prompt_md: How are option strategies classified?
fields.answer_md: Elementary strategies (long call, long put, short call, short put) and combinations. Combinations are either stock-plus-option (covered call, protective put, short stock with long call, short stock with short put) or option-plus-option (spreads, straddle, strangle, strap, strip).

fields.prompt_md: Covered call: construction, view and payoff shape.
fields.answer_md: Long stock plus a short call. Used when the investor fears a decline or expects only a small rise. The premium cushions a fall and adds income if the price stays below the strike; if the price rises sharply the short call eats the stock's gain, so profit is capped.

fields.prompt_md: Share bought at Rs 3,850; call written at strike 4,000 for Rs 80. Maximum profit and break-even?
fields.answer_md: Maximum profit = (4,000 - 3,850) + 80 = Rs 230, earned at any price from 4,000 upward. Break-even = 3,850 - 80 = Rs 3,770; below that price the position loses.

fields.prompt_md: Protective put: construction, view and payoff shape.
fields.answer_md: Long stock plus a long put. Used to insure against a fall while keeping upside. The put gains as the stock falls, so the loss is limited; beyond the premium the stock gains are retained. Works best when a moderate to sharp decline is feared.

fields.prompt_md: Share bought at Rs 310 with a put of strike 270 bought for Rs 2. Maximum loss and break-even?
fields.answer_md: Maximum loss = (310 - 270) + 2 = Rs 42, whatever the fall. Break-even = 310 + 2 = Rs 312; above that the position is profitable.

fields.prompt_md: Short stock plus long call: when and why?
fields.answer_md: Used by someone who has sold short and fears a price rise. The call gains as the price climbs, covering the loss on the short stock, so the loss is limited. Best against a large price appreciation.

fields.prompt_md: Short stock sold at Rs 300 with a call (strike 350) bought for Rs 5: maximum loss?
fields.answer_md: (350 - 300) + 5 = Rs 55, however high the price goes.

fields.prompt_md: Short stock plus short put: when and why?
fields.answer_md: Used by a short seller expecting a small decline. The put premium adds to the gain on the short stock, but once the price falls below the put's strike the put loses and offsets further gains, so gain is capped.

fields.definition_md: A position made by simultaneously buying and selling options of the same class (all calls or all puts) on the same underlying, differing in strike price, expiry or both. Buyers use spreads to cut the net cost of a trade; sellers use them to cap loss and reduce margin.

fields.prompt_md: Vertical, horizontal (calendar) and diagonal spreads: what differs between the legs?
fields.answer_md: Vertical: same expiry, different strikes. Horizontal or calendar: same strike, different expiries. Diagonal: both strike and expiry differ.

fields.prompt_md: How is a bull call spread built, and what are its risk, reward and break-even?
fields.answer_md: Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call. For a moderately bullish view. Risk: limited to the net debit paid. Reward: limited to the gap between strikes minus the net debit. Break-even: lower strike plus net debit.

fields.prompt_md: Buy Nifty call 4,100 at 172.45 and sell call 4,400 at 37.40. Give net debit, maximum gain and break-even.
fields.answer_md: Net debit = 172.45 - 37.40 = 135.05, which is also the maximum loss (price at or below 4,100). Maximum gain = 300 - 135.05 = 164.95 (price at or above 4,400). Break-even = 4,100 + 135.05 = 4,235.05.

fields.prompt_md: Which legs make up a bull put spread and what are its profit, loss and break-even?
fields.answer_md: Sell a higher-strike put and buy a lower-strike put. Moderately bullish. Receives a net credit, which is the maximum profit (price at or above the higher strike). Maximum loss = strike gap minus credit. Break-even = higher strike minus net credit.

fields.prompt_md: Sell put 4,000 at 21.45 and buy put 3,800 at 3.00. Net credit, break-even, maximum loss?
fields.answer_md: Net credit = 18.45 (maximum profit). Break-even = 4,000 - 18.45 = 3,981.55. Maximum loss = 200 - 18.45 = 181.55 (price at or below 3,800).

fields.prompt_md: Construct a bear call spread: when is it used, what is the best and worst outcome, and where is break-even?
fields.answer_md: Sell a lower-strike call and buy a higher-strike call. Used when the investor is mildly bearish or expects a range-bound market. Net credit is the maximum profit; maximum loss = strike gap minus credit; break-even = lower strike plus net credit.

fields.prompt_md: Sell call 2,600 at 154 and buy call 2,800 at 49. Net credit, break-even, maximum loss?
fields.answer_md: Net credit 105 (maximum profit, at or below 2,600). Break-even 2,600 + 105 = 2,705. Maximum loss = 200 - 105 = 95 (at or above 2,800).

fields.prompt_md: Bear put spread: construction, view, risk, reward.
fields.answer_md: Buy a higher-strike (ITM) put and sell a lower-strike (OTM) put, same expiry. Moderately bearish. Risk limited to the net premium paid; reward limited to the strike gap minus the net premium. Break-even = higher strike minus net debit.

fields.prompt_md: Buy put 2,800 at 132 and sell put 2,600 at 52. Net debit, maximum gain and break-even?
fields.answer_md: Net debit = 80 (maximum loss, at or above 2,800). Maximum gain = 200 - 80 = 120 (at or below 2,600). Break-even = 2,800 - 80 = 2,720.

fields.mnemonic: Bull buys low, bear buys high
fields.expands_md: In a vertical spread a bullish position buys the lower strike (and sells the higher); a bearish one buys the higher strike (and sells the lower). It holds for both calls and puts. Bull call and bear put are debit spreads; bull put and bear call are credit spreads.

fields.definition_md: An arbitrage position made of a bull call spread plus the matching bear put spread, with the same strikes and expiry. Its value at expiry is always the gap between the two strikes. If the box can be bought for less than that, the difference is a riskless profit.

fields.name: Box spread value and arbitrage gain
fields.variables_md: Net cost = net premium paid for the four legs: buy ITM call, sell OTM call, buy ITM put, sell OTM put.
fields.when_md: Worked example: strikes 40 and 50, total cost 950 per lot of 100 against expiry value 1,000, so profit 50.

fields.prompt_md: Calendar spread: construction and cash flow.
fields.answer_md: Opposite positions in two options of the same kind and same strike but different expiries; typically sell the near-dated option and buy the longer-dated one. A longer option costs more, so it needs an initial outlay.

fields.prompt_md: Diagonal spread: example.
fields.answer_md: Use options of different strike and different expiry, for example buy a longer-dated call with a lower strike and sell a shorter-dated call with a higher strike.

fields.prompt_md: Long call butterfly: construction, view, risk and reward.
fields.answer_md: Sell two ATM calls, buy one lower-strike (ITM) call and one higher-strike (OTM) call, with the middle strike halfway between the others. Neutral on direction and bearish on volatility. Risk: the net debit. Reward: the gap between adjacent strikes minus the net debit.

fields.prompt_md: Nifty 9,200: sell two 9,200 calls at 97.90, buy a 9,100 call at 141.55 and a 9,300 call at 64. Net debit and break-evens?
Short call butterfly: construction and when used.
fields.answer_md: Buy two ATM calls, sell one ITM and one OTM call. Gains a net credit (the maximum profit) when the investor expects a big move either way, so it is neutral on direction and bullish on volatility. Loss is limited to the strike gap minus the credit.

fields.prompt_md: Condor spread: long versus short.
fields.answer_md: A non-directional strategy that limits both gains and losses. A long condor profits from low volatility and little movement in the underlying; a short condor profits from high volatility and a large move either way.

fields.prompt_md: Long straddle: construction, view, risk, reward, break-even points.
fields.answer_md: Buy a call and a put with the same strike and expiry. Used when a large move is expected but its direction is not. Risk: the total premium paid. Reward: unlimited. Break-evens: strike plus net premium (upper) and strike minus net premium (lower).

fields.prompt_md: Short straddle: construction, view, risk and reward.
fields.answer_md: Sell a call and a put with the same strike and expiry. Used when little movement is expected (sideways market). Reward limited to the premium received; risk unlimited. Break-evens: strike plus and minus the net premium received.

fields.prompt_md: A trader sells an at-the-money straddle on USD/EUR at 1.2000 with call premium 0.035 and put premium 0.040. What is the result if spot is 1.2900 at expiry?
fields.answer_md: The call is exercised against him: loss 1.2900 - 1.2000 = 0.0900. Premium received 0.075. Net loss = 0.015 per unit. The put lapses.

fields.prompt_md: Strangle: how does it differ from a straddle, and what are its two forms?
fields.answer_md: A strangle uses a slightly OTM put and a slightly OTM call (different strikes, same expiry), so it costs less than a straddle but needs a bigger price move to pay. Long strangle: buy both; risk is the premium paid, reward unlimited. Short strangle: sell both; reward limited to premium received, risk unlimited.

fields.prompt_md: What is a strap and what market view does it express?
fields.answer_md: Two calls and one put with the same strike, expiry and underlying. It is a long straddle weighted towards the upside, used when the investor is bullish and also expects high volatility.

fields.prompt_md: What does a strip consist of, and when is it chosen?
fields.answer_md: Two puts and one call with the same strike, expiry and underlying. The mirror of a strap, used when the investor is bearish and expects high volatility.

fields.mnemonic: Strap = calls up, strip = puts down
fields.expands_md: A strap holds two calls and one put (bullish tilt); a strip holds two puts and one call (bearish tilt). Both use the same strike and expiry, so both are straddles with an extra leg.

fields.prompt_md: Name the strategy: (i) one call and one put, same strike, same expiry; (ii) two calls and one put, same strike; (iii) one call and two puts, same strike; (iv) one call and one put at different strikes (put lower, call higher).
fields.answer_md: (i) long straddle; (ii) strap; (iii) strip; (iv) strangle.

fields.prompt_md: Strap on a stock with strike 100, call premium 15 and put premium 10 (two calls, one put bought). Cost and break-evens?
fields.answer_md: Net cost = 2 x 15 + 10 = 40. Upside break-even: 100 + 40/2 = 120 (each extra rupee earns twice). Downside break-even: 100 - 40 = 60. Loss is greatest, equal to 40, if expiry is exactly at 100.

fields.prompt_md: Strip on the same stock (two puts and one call bought). Cost and break-evens?
fields.answer_md: Net cost = 2 x 10 + 15 = 35. Downside break-even: 100 - 35/2 = 82.5. Upside break-even: 100 + 35 = 135. Maximum loss 35 at an expiry price of 100.

fields.prompt_md: An investor buys a 42-strike call for Rs 2 and a 40-strike put for Rs 1 on the same expiry. How does it work out if the stock goes to 44, or to 35?
fields.answer_md: Total cost Rs 3. At 44 the call earns 2, net loss Rs 1. At 35 the put earns 5, net gain Rs 2. It is a long strangle, paying off only for a large move either way.

fields.prompt_md: Match market view to option strategy.
fields.answer_md: Moderately bullish: bull call spread or bull put spread. Moderately bearish: bear put spread or bear call spread. Large move, direction unknown: long straddle, long strangle or short butterfly. Little movement: short straddle, short strangle or long butterfly. Bullish with high volatility: strap; bearish with high volatility: strip.

fields.prompt_md: Lesson from comparing a 'buy in rising market' rule in spot with option choice: how is the right option chosen?
fields.answer_md: In the cash market only the direction matters. In the options market the expected price at expiry relative to the strike price matters: buy a call if expected price exceeds strike, a put if strike exceeds expected price. A rising market can still leave a call worthless if the expected price stays below the strike, and calls and puts can be profitable in both rising and falling markets.

fields.name: Put-call parity (European options)
fields.expression_md: $C + Xe^{-rt} = P + S_0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; C = P + S_0 - Xe^{-rt},\quad P = C + Xe^{-rt} - S_0$
fields.variables_md: $C$, $P$ = call and put premium with the same strike $X$ and expiry; $S_0$ = spot price; $Xe^{-rt}$ = present value of the strike.
fields.when_md: Holds under no-arbitrage for European options on the same underlying. It does not apply to American options. Equivalent view: a call plus a bond paying $X$ at expiry costs the same as a put plus the stock.

fields.prompt_md: Spot Rs 500, a 3-month call with strike 550 costs Rs 12, risk-free rate 8%. What is the put price on put-call parity?
If the quoted put is cheaper than the price implied by put-call parity, what arbitrage is available?
fields.answer_md: The put is underpriced. Sell the call, buy the put and the stock, funded by borrowing the amount spent net of the call premium. At expiry, whatever the price, either the put or the call lets the stock be sold at X; the sale proceeds exceed the loan repayment, locking in a risk-free profit. If the put is dearer, do the reverse.

fields.prompt_md: Manju Ltd: spot 650, call (strike 700) 85, put 110, rate 10%, 3 months. Is there an arbitrage?
fields.answer_md: Parity put = 85 + 700$e^{-0.025}$ - 650 = about 117.73, above the actual 110, so the put is undervalued. Sell the call at 85, buy the put at 110, buy the stock at 650, borrowing 675. At expiry the stock is sold for 700 either way, loan repayment is about 692, so net gain about Rs 8.

fields.prompt_md: Two meanings of 'option valuation' and the main models.
fields.answer_md: (1) The value of the option at maturity, which is what the holder receives on exercise. (2) The value at writing, which is the premium. The two main models for the premium are the binomial model and the Black-Scholes model.

fields.prompt_md: Explain the binomial option pricing model in brief.
fields.answer_md: It assumes the underlying can end at only two prices over a step: one above and one below the strike. It builds a tree of up and down moves, finds the option's payoff at the last nodes, takes the expected payoff using risk-neutral probabilities, and discounts it at the risk-free rate, rolling back to today.

fields.name: Binomial model: risk-neutral probability and growth factors
fields.variables_md: $u$, $d$ = up and down factors, $f$ = risk-free growth factor for one step, $p$ = risk-neutral probability of the up move.
fields.when_md: The study text loosely calls $p$ the 'implied volatility'. It is the risk-neutral probability of an up move, not volatility.

fields.name: Binomial model: value of a call and a put (one step)
fields.variables_md: $C_u$, $C_d$ = option payoff at the up and down prices (use $\max(S-X,0)$ for calls, $\max(X-S,0)$ for puts).
fields.when_md: For several steps, repeat the formula at every node, working backwards from expiry to today; do not set a node to zero merely because it is currently out of the money.

fields.prompt_md: Stock Rs 50 can go up or down 20% in 3 months; rate 8% continuous; strike 50. Value the call and the put by the binomial model.
Two-step binomial tree: stock 50, up/down 20% per 3-month step, rate 8%, strike 45. How is the call valued?
fields.answer_md: Final prices 72, 48, 32 give payoffs 27, 3 and 0. Roll back with p = 0.5505 and f = 1.0202: up node (60) = 15.89, down node (40) = 1.62, today = (15.89p + 1.62(1-p))/f = about 9.29. The put works out to about 2.52. Put-call parity checks the result (9.29 - 2.52 = 6.77 = 50 - 45$e^{-0.04}$).

fields.prompt_md: What is the option delta in the binomial (delta) method and how is the call valued with it?
fields.answer_md: Delta = $(C_u - C_d)/(S_u - S_d)$, the shares needed to replicate the option. When $C_d = 0$: $C = \Delta\,[\,S_0 - PV(S_d)\,]$, where $PV(S_d)=S_d e^{-rt}$. Generally $C=\Delta S_0 - PV(\Delta S_d - C_d)$, i.e. buy $\Delta$ shares and borrow the present value of $\Delta S_d - C_d$.

fields.prompt_md: Stock 110 will be 100 or 150 in 3 months; strike 120; rate 12%. Value the call and then the put.
fields.answer_md: Payoffs 0 and 30, so delta = 30/50 = 0.6. PV of the lower price = 100 / $e^0.03$ = 97.04. Call = 0.6 x (110 - 97.04) = Rs 7.78. Put by parity = 7.78 + 120/$e^0.03$ - 110 = Rs 14.23.

fields.prompt_md: Stock 110 moves to 90 or 135 in 3 months; strike 120; r = 8%. Value the call by the delta method.
fields.answer_md: Delta = 15/45 = 1/3. PV of 90 = 90/$e^0.02$ = 88.21. Call = (1/3) x (110 - 88.21) = about Rs 7.26. The risk-neutral formula gives the same figure (rounding aside).

fields.prompt_md: In a replicating (delta) hedge how many shares are held per call, and how many calls per share?
fields.answer_md: Hold delta shares for each call written (or buy 1/delta calls per share held). If delta is 0.5, buy one call for every 0.5 share or equivalently two calls hedge one share.

fields.prompt_md: Probabilities of up and down moves are given in a binomial problem, but the risk-free rate is not. How is it found?
fields.answer_md: Use (1 - p) = (u - f)/(u - d), giving f = u - (down probability) x (u - d). With u = 1.4, d = 0.8 and a down probability of 0.6, f = 1.04 for the step; r follows from $e^{r x step}$ = 1.04 (about 7.84% a year for a half-year step).

fields.prompt_md: State the assumptions of the Black-Scholes model.
fields.answer_md: No dividend on the stock; efficient market; no transaction costs or taxes; constant and known risk-free rate during the option's life; stock returns log-normally distributed; European exercise only.

fields.name: Black-Scholes value of a European call and put
fields.variables_md: $N(\cdot)$ = cumulative standard normal distribution; $S$ = spot; $X$ = strike; $r$ = continuous risk-free rate; $t$ = years to expiry.
fields.when_md: Non-dividend paying stock, European option. Put-call parity must hold between the two values.

fields.name: Black-Scholes d1 and d2
fields.variables_md: $\sigma$ = annual volatility (standard deviation) of the stock's return, $\ln$ = natural logarithm.
fields.when_md: Compute $d_1$ then $d_2$, look up the normal values, and substitute in the call or put formula.

fields.prompt_md: Stock 90, strike 80, r = 8%, volatility 23%, 6 months. Value the call and the put by Black-Scholes.
A European put: S = 50, X = 50, r = 10%, volatility 30%, 3 months, no dividend. What is the Black-Scholes price?
How is a known dividend handled in Black-Scholes?
fields.answer_md: Reduce the share price by the present value of the dividends expected during the option's life, then apply the formula to that adjusted price. For a Rs 1.50 dividend in 2 months and rate 10%, S0 falls from 50 to about 48.52.

fields.prompt_md: What is the intuition behind the Black-Scholes price?
fields.answer_md: An option can be replicated by a long position in the stock and a short position in a zero-coupon bond, rebalanced as the price moves. Black-Scholes sets the option price equal to that portfolio's value; any other price lets arbitrageurs bring it back.

fields.prompt_md: What are the Greeks and which four are used most?
fields.answer_md: Greeks measure how an option's price responds to changes in its drivers. The four most used are delta (underlying price), gamma (change in delta), theta (time) and vega (volatility); rho (interest rate) is the last and least used.

fields.mnemonic: Delta price, Gamma pace, Theta time, Vega volatility, Rho rate
fields.expands_md: Delta: option price against the underlying's price. Gamma: the pace at which delta changes. Theta: time decay. Vega: volatility. Rho: interest rate.

fields.name: Delta of an option
fields.expression_md: $\Delta = \dfrac{\text{Change in option price}}{\text{Change in price of underlying}}$
fields.variables_md: Call delta is positive and put delta is negative. For a call whose premium moved from 20 to 23 when the stock moved from 240 to 250, delta = 3 / 10 = 0.30.
fields.when_md: Also the number of units of the underlying to hold per option sold to build a riskless (delta-neutral) hedge.

fields.prompt_md: Typical delta values by moneyness.
fields.answer_md: Deep in-the-money: close to +1 for a call (or -1 for a put), never beyond that. At-the-money: about +/-0.5. Out-of-the-money: near zero.

fields.prompt_md: What is delta hedging and why must it be rebalanced?
fields.answer_md: Delta hedging means holding the underlying and options in proportion to delta so the combined position is riskless. Delta keeps changing with the price and with time, so the position stays delta-neutral only for a short time and must be adjusted periodically.

fields.prompt_md: What does gamma measure and how does its size affect rebalancing?
fields.answer_md: Gamma is the rate of change of delta for a change in the underlying price (the second derivative of the option price, also called curvature). Low gamma: delta changes slowly, so little rebalancing. High gamma: delta is very sensitive, so frequent rebalancing is needed.

fields.prompt_md: Which Greek measures sensitivity of an option's price to the volatility of the underlying, and what are its features?
fields.answer_md: Vega. It is the change in premium for a unit change in volatility, lies between zero and infinity for both calls and puts, is greatest for at-the-money options with long time to expiry, and is positive for the option buyer and negative for the seller.

fields.prompt_md: Which Greek measures the time decay of an option, and how does it behave?
fields.answer_md: Theta: the change in option price as time passes, usually measured per day. Its value ranges between zero and the total value of the option; it works against the holder and in favour of the writer, and options lose value as expiry approaches.

fields.prompt_md: What does rho measure and what is its sign for different positions?
fields.answer_md: Rho: change in option value for a one-percentage-point change in the interest rate. A rate rise lifts call values and trims put values. Rho is positive if you are long a call or short a put, and negative if you are short a call or long a put.

fields.definition_md: An agreement between two parties to exchange sequences of cash flows over a set period, where at least one leg depends on an uncertain variable such as an interest rate, exchange rate, equity price or commodity price. Equivalent views: a bundle of forward contracts, or owning one bond while being short another.

fields.prompt_md: Why are swaps not exchange-traded, and what follows from that?
fields.answer_md: They are customised OTC contracts between private parties, mostly firms and financial institutions. Because there is no exchange or clearing house, each side carries the risk that the other defaults, so default risk is higher than for futures or options.

fields.prompt_md: List the main features of a swap.
fields.answer_md: Counterparties who exchange cash flows; dealers or brokers who facilitate; present values of the flows estimated upfront; less documentation; modest transaction cost (commission); done only where both gain; cannot be terminated unilaterally; higher default risk as it is bilateral.

fields.prompt_md: Name the main types of financial swaps.
fields.answer_md: Interest rate swaps, currency swaps, equity swaps and credit default swaps.

fields.definition_md: An agreement to exchange interest and principal payments in one currency for interest and principal in another currency of the same maturity. Because principal is exchanged at the start and re-exchanged at the end, it creates a larger credit exposure than an interest rate swap.

A special type of total return swap with a stock, basket or index as underlying. One party passes on the equity's appreciation and dividends and receives a guaranteed return plus any fall in the equity's value.

fields.prompt_md: State the benefits of swaps.
fields.answer_md: Cheaper borrowing through comparative advantage (Ricardo's theory); access to new markets; hedging of interest or currency risk; correcting asset-liability mismatches; and extra brokerage income for intermediaries.

fields.prompt_md: Explain how swaps lower borrowing costs by the theory of comparative cost.
fields.answer_md: Each borrower swaps the advantage it enjoys in one market for the other's advantage in the other market, so that each ends up with funds cheaper than it could raise on its own.

fields.prompt_md: How can a swap correct an asset-liability mismatch? Give an example.
fields.answer_md: A bank holding a fixed-rate asset funded by floating-rate liabilities loses if rates rise. By paying fixed and receiving floating in a swap, its fixed receipts on assets match the fixed payment to the counterparty, and the floating receipt matches the floating cost of liabilities.

fields.definition_md: A contract in which two parties exchange interest payments or receipts in the same currency on different bases for a specified maturity. No principal changes hands: the notional amount is used only to calculate the payments.

fields.prompt_md: Name the three key features of an interest rate swap.
fields.answer_md: Notional principal (the amount on which interest is calculated, never exchanged); the fixed rate, quoted by banks as the rate they will pay (bid) or receive (offer); and the floating rate, tied to a market index such as LIBOR, MIBOR or the Treasury bill rate.

fields.prompt_md: What is a plain vanilla swap?
fields.answer_md: The simplest interest rate swap: fixed-for-floating in the same currency. It is also called a coupon swap or fixed-to-floating swap. One party pays a fixed rate and receives a floating rate on the same notional, the other the opposite.

fields.prompt_md: List other kinds of interest rate swaps besides plain vanilla.
fields.answer_md: Zero coupon to floating; alternative floating rate; floating-to-floating; forward swap; rate-capped swap; extendable swap.

fields.prompt_md: Describe a zero-coupon-to-floating swap, a forward swap and a rate-capped swap.
fields.answer_md: Zero-coupon to floating: the fixed-rate party makes a single bullet payment at the end while the floating-rate party pays periodically. Forward swap: payments start at a specified future date. Rate-capped swap: the floating payments are capped, and the floating-rate payer pays an upfront fee to the fixed-rate party for the cap.

fields.prompt_md: Alternative floating-rate swap, floating-to-floating swap and extendable swap: what are they?
fields.answer_md: Alternative floating rate: the floating reference can be switched to other benchmarks (three-month rate, commercial paper, T-bill). Floating-to-floating: each party pays a different floating rate, often used by non-US banks to manage dollar exposure. Extendable: the parties may extend the life of the swap.

fields.prompt_md: Firm X holds $100 million of fixed-rate mortgages yielding 9.5% funded at LIBOR + 0.5%. It pays a bank 7.5% fixed and receives LIBOR. What is its cost of funds and locked-in spread?
fields.answer_md: Cost of funds = 7.5% + 0.5% = 8% fixed (the LIBOR it pays on its loan is covered by the LIBOR it receives). Locked-in spread = 9.5% - 8% = 1.5%, no longer exposed to rate moves.

fields.prompt_md: In the same deal Firm Y receives 7.4% fixed and pays LIBOR to the bank; what does the bank earn?
fields.answer_md: The bank receives 7.5% from X and pays 7.4% to Y, with the LIBOR legs cancelling. Net gain 0.10% on the 100 million notional, i.e. 100,000 a year.

fields.definition_md: A combination of an option and a swap. The buyer gets the right to enter an interest rate swap by a specified future date, and the agreement states whether the buyer will pay fixed or receive fixed. If exercised, the writer becomes the buyer's counterparty. Types: call swaption (callable swap) and put swaption (puttable swap).

fields.prompt_md: Under the study text, what do callable and puttable swaps give?
fields.answer_md: A callable swap gives the fixed-rate payer the right to terminate the swap before maturity, making the writer the fixed-rate receiver and floating-rate payer. A puttable swap gives the floating-rate payer the right to terminate, making the writer the floating receiver and fixed payer.

fields.name: Value of a plain vanilla interest rate swap
fields.variables_md: $B_{fix}$ = present value of the fixed-coupon bond (all fixed payments plus the notional) at current zero rates; $B_{float}$ = value of the floating-rate bond, which is the next floating payment plus notional discounted from the next payment date (it resets to par then).
fields.when_md: For the party paying fixed and receiving floating the value is $B_{float} - B_{fix}$. After inception an off-market swap can be positive or negative but is not zero.

fields.prompt_md: A bank pays six-month LIBOR and receives 8% on 100 million notional. Remaining life 1.25 years, zero rates 10%, 10.5% and 11% for 3, 9 and 15 months. Last floating payment 5.1m. Find the swap's value.
Outline the steps to design an interest rate swap that exploits comparative advantage.
fields.answer_md: 1) Find each firm's rate in the fixed market and in the floating market. 2) Compute the fixed-rate gap and the floating-rate gap between the two firms. 3) Total swap gain = difference between the two gaps. 4) Deduct the intermediary's commission. 5) Split the remainder as agreed. 6) The firm with the greater comparative advantage borrows in that market; the other borrows in the other market. 7) Compute each firm's net cost.

fields.name: Total gain from an interest rate swap
fields.variables_md: $F_A$, $F_B$ = fixed rates available to firms A and B; $L_A$, $L_B$ = their floating-rate spreads.
fields.when_md: If the two quality spreads are equal the gain is zero and no beneficial swap exists. From this subtract the commission paid to the intermediary before splitting.

fields.prompt_md: Why is the market where each company borrows decided by relative, not absolute, advantage?
fields.answer_md: Even the stronger company has an advantage in both markets; the swap gain arises from the difference in the size of that advantage. The stronger firm borrows where its advantage is greater, the weaker where its disadvantage is smaller. The firms' views on interest rates do not determine the structure; they only decide who wants which rate.

fields.prompt_md: Somnath: fixed 10%, floating MIBOR - 0.5%. Amal: fixed 12.5%, floating MIBOR + 1%. Gain is shared 60:40 and Somnath wants floating, Amal wants fixed. Find effective rates and savings on 100 crore for 7 years.
fields.answer_md: Fixed gap 2.5%, floating gap 1.5%, so gain = 1.0%. Somnath gets 0.6%, Amal 0.4%. Somnath borrows fixed (10%) and ends at MIBOR - 1.10%; Amal borrows floating and ends at 12.5% - 0.4% = 12.10% fixed. Savings: Rs 60 lakh and Rs 40 lakh a year, i.e. Rs 4.2 crore and Rs 2.8 crore over seven years.

fields.prompt_md: PQR: fixed 12%, floating LIBOR+0.1%. DEF: fixed 13.4%, floating LIBOR+0.6%. PQR wants floating, DEF wants fixed. A bank takes 0.5% and the rest is split equally. Find effective rates.
fields.answer_md: Fixed gap 1.4%, floating gap 0.5%, gain 0.9%. After the bank's 0.5%, 0.4% remains, 0.2% each. PQR borrows fixed at 12% and ends at LIBOR - 0.1%; DEF borrows floating and ends at 13.2% fixed.

fields.prompt_md: A pays fixed 9.5% but wants floating at no more than LIBOR (floating alternative LIBOR + 2%); B can raise fixed at 13.5% and floating at LIBOR + 2%, and cannot pay over 12% fixed. How is a bank-arranged swap shared?
fields.answer_md: Fixed gap is 4% (13.5 - 9.5) and floating gap is zero, so the total gain is 4%. A needs 2% (LIBOR + 2% down to LIBOR), B needs 1.5% (13.5% down to 12%) and the bank keeps the balance of 0.5%. A pays LIBOR, B pays 12% fixed all-in.

fields.prompt_md: When can no swap be structured between two companies?
fields.answer_md: When the difference between their fixed-rate costs equals the difference between their floating-rate costs, the net gain is zero and neither side can benefit.

fields.definition_md: A contract in which the buyer pays periodic premiums to the seller and receives a payoff if the reference debt instrument defaults or suffers a specified credit event. It is a way of swapping default risk and can be written on bonds, mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities or loans.

fields.prompt_md: State the uses of credit default swaps.
fields.answer_md: Hedging default risk (for example by a bank holding loans, or to reduce concentration to a borrower or industry without disturbing the customer), speculation, and arbitrage such as capital structure arbitrage.

fields.prompt_md: A pension fund holds Rs 10 million of 5-year bonds and buys a CDS at 200 basis points. What are the net proceeds with no default, and with default after 3 years (zero recovery)?
fields.answer_md: No default: premium 10m x 2% x 5 = Rs 1m, so net proceeds Rs 9m. Default after 3 years: premium 0.6m, CDS pays 10m, so net proceeds Rs 9.4m. Either way the default risk is avoided.

fields.prompt_md: What is capital structure arbitrage using CDS?
fields.answer_md: It exploits mispricing between a company's debt and equity. Share price and CDS spread should be negatively correlated. If bad news cuts the share price but the CDS spread has not moved, an investor buys CDS protection (long the spread) expecting the spread to widen.

fields.definition_md: A derivative priced off interest rates in some form: the rates themselves, interest-bearing instruments or rate indices. Users hedge rate risk with it, fine-tune a risk profile, or speculate on the direction of rates.

fields.prompt_md: List the principal interest rate derivatives.
fields.answer_md: Forward rate agreements, interest rate futures, interest rate options, interest rate swaps, caps, floors and collars.

fields.definition_md: A contract, usually between a bank and a customer, to pay or receive the difference between an agreed fixed rate and the actual rate on a future fixing date, on a notional amount for a specified period. No lending or borrowing takes place; only the rate is fixed.

fields.prompt_md: How does buying an FRA protect a borrower?
fields.answer_md: The borrower who will need funds later buys an FRA at a fixed rate. If the market rate at settlement is above the FRA rate the seller (bank) pays the difference to the buyer, offsetting the higher borrowing cost; if it is lower, the buyer pays the difference. Selling an FRA protects a depositor against falling rates.

fields.name: FRA settlement amount
fields.variables_md: $N$ = notional, $R$ = reference (settlement) rate, $K$ = FRA rate, $\alpha$ = day-count fraction of the contract period (for example days/360).
fields.when_md: Positive: seller pays buyer; negative: buyer pays seller. The interest difference is discounted at the reference rate because it is settled upfront, not at the end of the period.

fields.prompt_md: What does a '3 x 6' or '2 x 8' FRA mean?
fields.answer_md: The first number is the months until the contract period starts (the settlement date) and the second is months to its end. A 3 x 6 FRA fixes the rate on a three-month period beginning three months from now; a 2 x 8 FRA fixes a six-month rate starting in two months.

fields.prompt_md: Why is the FRA settlement discounted?
fields.answer_md: Interest on an actual deposit or loan is paid at the end of the period, while an FRA is settled in cash at the start of that period. The interest difference is therefore discounted back over the period at the prevailing reference rate.

fields.prompt_md: A bank sells a 3 x 6 FRA on 30 million at 5.5%, 92-day period. Who pays whom, and how much, if the settlement rate is 4.875% and if it is 6.125%?
fields.answer_md: At 4.875% the buyer pays the seller about 47,326: (0.04875 - 0.055) x 92/360 x 30,000,000 / (1 + 0.04875 x 92/360). At 6.125% the seller pays the buyer about 47,178.

fields.prompt_md: A firm rolls over a 25 million loan priced at LIBOR for 3 months and fears a rise. It buys a 3 x 6 FRA at 6%. What is the settlement if the rate is 6.25% (90 days)?
How does an FRA differ from an interest rate cap or floor?
fields.answer_md: An FRA fixes a rate and settles both ways (the buyer may have to pay), with no premium. A cap or floor is an option: the buyer pays an upfront premium and only receives payments, never owing anything if rates move the right way.

fields.definition_md: A standardised, exchange-traded contract to buy or sell a debt instrument on a future date at a price fixed today. At NSE the underlying is a government bond or Treasury bill; all the contracts are cash settled.

fields.prompt_md: What are the main features of interest rate futures?
fields.answer_md: Exchange-traded and cash settled; small contract size for wide participation; transparent, with settlement at clean price; available across yields, benchmarks and maturities; centralised clearing with guaranteed settlement; cheaper and easier access to rate trading.

fields.prompt_md: List the uses of interest rate futures.
fields.answer_md: Hedging, managing the duration of a portfolio, locking in yields, calendar-spread speculation, arbitrage and directional trading.

fields.prompt_md: How are interest rate futures used to hedge a debt fund when yields are expected to rise?
fields.answer_md: Rising yields cut bond prices and the fund's NAV. The holder sells (shorts) interest rate futures; a fall in futures price gives a gain to offset the NAV loss without redeeming units. Example: loss on 10,000 units (13.30 to 13.15) = 1,500; gain on 2,000 bonds (104.20 to 103.50) = 1,400; net loss only 100.

fields.prompt_md: Directional trading with interest rate futures: which position profits when yields are expected to rise?
fields.answer_md: Short futures, because bond prices and futures prices move inversely to yields. Example: 10 lots of 2,000 bonds sold at 104.45 and bought back at 103.90 give 2,000 x 10 x 0.55 = Rs 11,000.

fields.prompt_md: What is a calendar spread in interest rate futures?
