fields.answer_md: Simultaneously buying one delivery month of a contract and selling another delivery month of the same underlying on the same exchange (an inter-delivery spread), profiting from the change in the gap between the two prices.

fields.definition_md: An option whose value depends on interest rates or interest-rate instruments. A call gives the right to gain if rates rise above the strike; a put gives the right to gain if rates fall below it. The holder needs a move large enough to cover the premium.

An agreement in which the buyer pays an upfront premium and receives a payment for each period in which the reference rate is above the agreed cap (strike) rate. It places a ceiling on the cost of floating-rate borrowing. The buyer has no obligation if rates stay below the cap.

fields.prompt_md: State the features and constituents of interest rate caps and floors.
fields.answer_md: The buyer pays a premium for the right to receive the interest difference; no liability for the buyer if rates move favourably; behaves like an option. Terms cover 1 to 10 years with resets and payments commonly 3 or 6 months apart. Constituents: notional principal, interest rate index (such as LIBOR), cap or floor rate (the strike), and the agreement period with reset and payment dates.

fields.name: Cap and floor settlement per period
fields.variables_md: $N$ = notional, $r$ = index rate at reset, $r_c$ = cap rate, $r_f$ = floor rate, $dt$ = days between reset and payment date.
fields.when_md: The seller pays the buyer when the index is above the cap rate, or below the floor rate.

fields.definition_md: A contract in which the buyer pays a premium and receives payments for each period in which the reference rate is below the floor rate. It guarantees a minimum return on a floating-rate investment and suits a lender or depositor who fears falling rates.

fields.prompt_md: Who buys a cap and who buys a floor?
fields.answer_md: A borrower on floating rates fearing a rate rise buys a cap. A lender or investor on floating rates fearing a rate fall buys a floor.

fields.definition_md: A cap and a floor combined: the buyer buys a cap and simultaneously sells a floor, so the floating rate is held within a band. The premium received on the floor offsets the premium paid for the cap; if equal, it is a zero-premium collar. It gives up some benefit from falling rates in return for lower cost.

fields.prompt_md: Collar: what does the buyer give up and gain?
fields.answer_md: The buyer is protected above the cap rate but, having sold the floor, must pay the dealer if rates fall below the floor rate. The cost of the cap is reduced or removed by the floor premium, but the benefit of falling rates stops at the floor.

fields.prompt_md: A borrower of 200 million floats at LIBOR + 0.25%, buys a 3-year cap at 9% with premium 4 million (amortised equally). LIBOR at the three resets is 9.5%, 8.5% and 10%. What does the cap pay each year?
fields.answer_md: Year 1: 200m x 0.5% = 1.0 million. Year 2: nil, since 8.5% is below 9%. Year 3: 200m x 1% = 2.0 million. The premium costs about 1.33 million a year.

fields.prompt_md: A deposit of 200 million earns LIBOR + 0.5%. A 3-year floor at 8% costs 3 million. LIBOR at the resets is 7.5%, 9% and 7%. What does the floor pay?
fields.answer_md: Year 1: 200m x 0.5% = 1.0 million. Year 2: nil (9% is above 8%). Year 3: 200m x 1% = 2.0 million. Premium amortises at 1.0 million a year.

fields.prompt_md: Cap of 400 million at 9% costs 0.65% and a floor at 4% costs 0.69%. What are the net savings if rates hit 10%, and how many floors must be sold to pay for the cap?
fields.answer_md: Cap premium = 2.6 million; at 10% it pays 400m x 1% = 4 million, net saving 1.4 million. Floors to sell: 2.6m / 0.0069 = about 376.8 million of floors, so the premium received equals the cap's cost.

fields.text_md: Long forward payoff = {{c1::spot at delivery minus forward price}}; short forward payoff = {{c2::forward price minus spot at delivery}}; both break even when spot equals {{c3::the forward price}}.

Futures margin: the original deposit is the {{c1::initial margin}}, the minimum balance to be kept is the {{c2::maintenance margin}}, and the top-up that restores the initial level after a margin call is the {{c3::variation margin}}.
Basis = {{c1::futures price minus spot price}}; in a normal market it is {{c2::positive}}, in an inverted market {{c3::negative}}, and as expiry nears futures and spot {{c4::converge}}.
To hedge a long portfolio with index futures, {{c1::sell}} futures worth {{c2::beta}} times the portfolio value; to raise beta, {{c3::buy}} index futures.
Break-even price: call = {{c1::strike plus premium}}; put = {{c2::strike minus premium}}.
{{c1::Delta}} measures sensitivity to the underlying's price, {{c2::gamma}} the rate of change of delta, {{c3::theta}} time decay, {{c4::vega}} volatility and {{c5::rho}} the interest rate.
A long straddle buys a {{c1::call}} and a {{c2::put}} at the {{c3::same}} strike; a strap holds {{c4::two calls and one put}}; a strip holds {{c5::two puts and one call}}.
A plain vanilla swap exchanges {{c1::fixed}} for {{c2::floating}} interest payments; the notional principal is {{c3::never exchanged}}.
A cap protects a {{c1::borrower}} from rising rates; a floor protects a {{c2::lender or depositor}} from falling rates; a collar means buying a {{c3::cap}} and selling a {{c4::floor}}.
A 3 x 6 FRA fixes a {{c1::three}}-month rate that starts {{c2::three}} months from now.
Binomial model: p = (f - d)/(u - d), where f is {{c1::e^{rt}}} and u and d are the {{c2::up and down}} factors.
A covered call is {{c1::long stock plus a short call}}; a protective put is {{c2::long stock plus a long put}}.
Bull spreads {{c1::buy}} the lower strike and bear spreads {{c2::buy}} the higher strike; a long butterfly sells {{c3::two}} middle-strike calls.
